transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2027-10-06 14:00 PT
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Ellen Park (AegisReg), Marcus Lee (AegisReg), Priya Sharma (AegisReg)

Auto-generated Summary (brief):
AegisReg Labs is a regulated diagnostics provider exploring a private, air-gapped deployment for model inference. Primary concerns: offline update mechanics, firmware signing, no inbound network, hardware limitations (NVMe capacity, no NVLink), KMS/HSM integration for key custody, and auditability for regulators. Redwood AE/SE walked through deployment patterns (private control plane vs fully offline), suggested canary strategies, and committed to a PoC to validate performance on their constrained nodes.

Topics:
- Deployment topology options (private control plane vs fully disconnected)
- Update/patch workflow and signature verification
- Hardware constraints: GPU type restrictions, NVMe capacity, lack of internet
- Compliance checkboxes: SOC2, audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, binary signing
- Rollout/rollback and canary strategies in air-gapped environments

Action items (captured in metadata as well): see action_items field.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call, I have Samir from our infra team, and you folks?
[00:08] Marcus (AegisReg): Marcus here, I'll be doing the ops intake; Ellen and Priya will lead compliance and architecture.
[00:14] Ellen (AegisReg): Hi. Good to meet you. We're trying to understand how Redwood can work in a completely air-gapped datacenter, we have strict auditors.
[00:22] Maya: Totally, that's the core of why we're here. High level, Redwood supports Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. For private air-gapped we have two patterns: a private control plane with egress-limited connectors, or a fully disconnected node set where updates are delivered via signed artifacts. We'll walk both.
[00:38] Samir (Redwood SE): Quick caveat: in fully disconnected mode we can't do remote telemetry — you'll get local logs and you push them out via approved channels. There's a signed update flow we use with HSM-backed keys.
[00:49] Priya (AegisReg): When you say HSM, are you talking about on-prem HSMs? We can't give keys to cloud KMS.
[00:55] Samir: Yes, on-prem HSM or customer-managed KMS is supported. Redwood's agent can verify signatures from your HSM public key. The flow is: build artifact, sign with your HSM, ship CD image, node verifies signature before install.
[01:08] Ellen: Ok, auditors will want to see chain-of-custody and signed manifests.
[01:12] Maya: We have an audit log format and can map to your controls. There may be slight word mismatches in the sample logs we provide but we can align fields.
[01:20] Marcus: Our big constrain — we have older blades; no NVLink, only PCIe T4 GPUs and a small NVMe pool (two drives, 2TB total) — how does Redwood handle KV cache given the limited disk?
[01:32] Samir: Good question. We can configure the KV caching to be in-memory or on local NVMe; for small NVMe we'd recommend a memory-first configuration and aggressive evictions, and use quantized models to reduce KV size. There's tradeoffs in latency. Also batching behavior changes.
[01:46] Ellen: Quantization — do you support int8? Some of the clinical models we use are sensitive to precision loss.
[01:52] Samir: Yes, we support multiple quantization profiles. For clinical-grade models, we usually recommend mixed precision or 4-bit where acceptable; we can run an eval on your prompt set in the PoC to measure quality regressions.
[02:06] Priya: About the update window: our policy is quarterly security patches; we don't allow unscheduled updates.
[02:12] Maya: Understood. Our signed-update flow can support scheduled rollouts; you control when nodes accept updates. We also support a canary policy that runs locally — choose a single node or cluster segment for canary, validate, then propagate offline.
[02:26] Marcus: How do you do rollbacks in an air-gapped setup?
[02:29] Samir: Rollback is simply a signed artifact that's marked as the active image; you keep previous images in your private registry (or store) — nodes can be instructed to revert to an older signed image. Important is you maintain the signatures and version metadata.
[02:41] Ellen: Do you provide a console for this or is it all command-line?
[02:45] Maya: For fully air-gapped we ship a local console binary that uses the same APIs as our hosted console but runs locally and integrates with your user directory (SAML/SSO if you run an IdP on-prem). For customers who want the private control plane, we host the control plane in a VPC with restricted peering.
[03:02] Priya: SAML is fine, but we need RBAC mapping to our AD groups.
[03:07] Samir: We map SAML group assertions to role mappings. We can also integrate with LDAP directly in fully-onprem deployments.
[03:15] Marcus: Network-wise, the nodes have zero inbound from the internet; they can send outbound via a bastion — but we prefer no outbound at all.
[03:23] Maya: If there is zero outbound, then telemetry and remote debugging won't be available and everything must be pulled via secure media. That's the fully disconnected model. We'll provide checksumed artifacts and a verification tool.
[03:36] Ellen: The auditors will press on firmware and BIOS updates — our process requires cryptographic validation of firmware and a documented chain-of-custody.
[03:45] Samir: We recommend signing firmware updates separately and treating them outside the Redwood update pipeline. Redwood's runtime will verify the model/artifact signatures but not the server firmware; that's a separate process you already have. We can note the requirement in our runbook.
[03:59] Marcus: Any minimum hardware requirements? We're on older gen T4s with 16GB memory each and 128GB RAM per host.
[04:07] Samir: Not strict minimums; depends on model size and throughput. For low-latency chat models we'd suggest at least 24GB vRAM for reasonable performance, but quantized models will run on 16GB. We'll run exact sizing during PoC.
[04:20] Priya: Isolation: we need guaranteed tenant separation and per-customer audit trails — we house multiple regulated workloads in the same cage.
[04:28] Maya: On private deployments we provision per-tenant namespaces, enforce RBAC, and produce per-tenant audit logs. In fully disconnected setups you'll need to aggregate logs from nodes periodically for central retention; we can provide the schema for that.
[04:40] Ellen: How do you handle model rollouts? We have an internal governance board that must approve models and prompts.
[04:47] Samir: We support version pinning and rollouts — deploy a model to a canary group, run your evals, and promote. The private console includes a model catalog and rollout controls. For audit purposes we can attach an approval artifact (signed) to the rollout event.
[05:00] Marcus: Licensing — do we need a persistent connection for license checks?
[05:05] Maya: No. For private/offline we use license bundles that are signed and provisioned to nodes. They expire at a defined window but don't require live heartbeat unless you opt in.
[05:15] Ellen: Encryption at rest, tokenization, and key custody — we need separation of duties.
[05:20] Samir: You can bring your own KMS/HSM. The node stores secrets encrypted and the keys never leave your HSM. We support envelope encryption, and can show the KMS integration doc.
[05:33] Priya: One red flag for auditors is unattended fallback to cloud if local capacity is exceeded. Does Redwood have auto-failover to hosted if you run out?
[05:41] Maya: Not by default. For private/offline, we only fail within the private infra. Fallback to hosted requires explicit configuration and consent; it's not automatic.
[05:51] Marcus: Performance: can we run batch inference for non-sensitive workloads? That would help cost.
[05:56] Samir: Yes, you can schedule batch jobs locally. Batching reduces per-token cost but increases latency. In the PoC we can show batch vs real-time comparisons.
[06:07] Ellen: Regarding logs and retention — auditors want immutable logs for 7 years.
[06:12] Maya: We produce logs that can be exported in an append-only format; for immutability you'd hook them to your WORM storage. We'll include an export guide.
[06:22] Marcus: Ok, walk us through a typical offline update flow — step by step.
[06:26] Samir: Sure — Build and sign artifact (customer or Redwood build), produce manifest with SHA256, transfer via secure media, node ingest validates signature against HSM public key, verifies manifest, stops service, applies update in an atomic way, runs post-checks, restarts, and writes signed audit entry. If post-checks fail, node reverts to previous image.
[06:48] Ellen: Any manual steps that are commonly missed?
[06:50] Samir: People forget to sync clocks for timestamped signatures and not preserving the old image or signature store. Also, key rotation needs coordination.
[06:58] Priya: How do you handle CRS/historical artifact access for auditors?
[07:02] Maya: We can provide a signed artifacts registry export and per-deployment manifest history. In disconnected setups you'd need to retain those artifacts in your own archival storage; we can script the export.
[07:16] Marcus: About support SLAs — in an air-gapped site, what's covered?
[07:20] Maya: Our enterprise support covers guidance, runbooks, and remote help via shipped debug bundles. We also have on-site options via engineering visits under an enterprise contract.
[07:31] Ellen: When we talk about on-site, auditors might require background checks for vendor engineers.
[07:36] Maya: That's common — we can do vetted personnel and NDAs; it's part of enterprise procurement.
[07:44] Marcus: Any regulatory precedents in healthcare or diagnostics where you've gone through this?
[07:49] Samir: Yes, we've done several private on-prem deployments for clinical labs and imaging companies — different names, but similar patterns: signed updates, HSM integration, no outbound telemetry. We can share redacted case studies.
[08:01] Priya: Can we see sample audit logs and signed manifests?
[08:05] Maya: We'll send a runbook and samples after this call.
[08:08] Ellen: Good.
[08:10] [short pause]
[10:30] Marcus: Jumping ahead — what's the timeline for a PoC? We have an internal target to decide by mid-November.
[10:36] Maya: If we start now, we can do a two-week PoC: week 1 for sizing and onboarding, week 2 for performance runs and validation. That would fit a mid-November decision.
[10:46] Priya: Stakeholders we'll involve: compliance team, architecture board, and ops — we'll also assign a single POC owner.
[10:54] Maya: Great. For the PoC we'll need hardware spec sheet, sample prompts/eval set, and a maintenance window for initial install.
[11:02] Marcus: Maintenance windows: we only allow installs on the 2nd Saturday of month; can the PoC fit that?
[11:08] Samir: For PoC we can do a staged demo in a lab environment first; production install can wait for your maintenance window. The lab can be an identical image you ship to us.
[11:19] Ellen: About telemetry again — is there any metadata that leaves the site by default?
[11:24] Maya: No by default in fully disconnected mode. If you pick private control plane with limited peering, we can send anonymized telemetry but it's opt-in.
[11:33] Priya: How do you protect model IP? We train models in cloud but the inference artifacts are sensitive.
[11:40] Samir: The inference artifacts are signed and encrypted; we don't extract model weights out of your environment. For private control plane, you can still host artifacts in your own registry.
[11:50] Marcus: What about software supply chain: do you sign third-party libs?
[11:54] Samir: We maintain SBOMs for our images. For third-party libs we include SBOM entries and version pins; we can provide SBOMs for auditors.
[12:07] Ellen: Anything else from your side that we should flag for procurement?
[12:11] Maya: Procurement will want pricing options: flat fee for private + support tiers, and PoC costs. We'll include that in the follow-up.
[12:19] Priya: Do you have specific language for contracts about air-gapped liability and data residency?
[12:24] Maya: Yes, we have addenda for air-gapped deployments and enterprise SLAs; legal can share after NDA.
[12:33] [crosstalk] Marcus: Ok, so immediate deliverables?
[12:36] Maya: Runbook, signed-update doc, sample audit logs, PoC plan.
[12:40] Ellen: And timelines for PoC.
[12:43] Samir: We'll also ask for a hardware spec sheet and a representative model or prompt set.
[12:49] Marcus: We'll get that to you.
[12:52] Maya: Great. Any other technical blockers you foresee?
[12:56] Priya: Key custody is the one; also the limited NVMe.
[13:01] Samir: We'll size for NVMe limits and recommend memory-first KV caching plus model quantization and batching tradeoffs.
[13:10] Marcus: If performance is unacceptable on existing T4s, is there a recommended refresh path?
[13:15] Maya: We can propose a phased hardware uplift — keep some capacity on current nodes for non-critical workloads and provision a few upgraded nodes for low-latency services. That fits your maintenance window.
[13:27] Ellen: For audit purposes, can you provide sample evidence of SOC2 controls?
[13:31] Maya: We'll share our SOC2 type II summary and a mapping doc to show how Redwood features map to control objectives.
[13:38] Priya: Who will be our technical contact?
[13:41] Maya: Samir will be SE lead; he'll run the PoC and technical runbook. I'm the commercial owner.
[13:47] Samir: I'll follow up with a PoC checklist and some sizing scripts.
[13:52] Marcus: Great.
[14:00] [longer silence, side conversations fade]
[20:15] Ellen: One more question: licensing for multiple isolated cages — we want per-cage tenancy.
[20:21] Maya: We can issue per-cage license bundles, each with its own signing and expiry. That avoids cross-cage communication.
[20:30] Marcus: How is metering handled if there's no telemetry?
[20:34] Maya: Metering is done via usage artifacts you export — token counts and timestamps are local and signed; you provide the export for billing reconciliation.
[20:44] Priya: Nice.
[21:00] Maya: Ok, last quick topic — vulnerability disclosure and emergency patching.
[21:05] Samir: We have an emergency patch flow that can produce an offline signed hotfix. It still requires a maintenance window from your side to apply.
[21:15] Ellen: We'll need proof of that flow in writing.
[21:18] Maya: We'll include it in the runbook.
[21:22] [short wrap-up]
[22:00] Maya: To recap: Redwood will send runbook, signed-update flow doc, SOC2 summary, sample logs, and PoC plan. Samir will prepare PoC scripts and sizing. AegisReg will send hardware specs, sample prompts, and confirm POC owner and maintenance window.
[22:25] Marcus: Sounds good. Can we get that in writing by Friday?
[22:28] Maya: Yes, I'll send the doc pack by Friday EOD.
[22:32] Priya: We'll review and circle back with the procurement timeline.
[22:36] Ellen: Thanks everyone.
[22:38] Maya: Thank you. Talk soon.
[22:42] [call ends]
